lead: A throttling calorimeter measures steam dryness without collecting water. Wet steam at pressure p₁ passes through a throttle to a lower pressure p₂ and leaves superheated. The steady flow energy equation, with no work, little heat loss and small kinetic and potential energy changes, gives h₁ = h₂. Steam tables turn the outlet p₂ and T₂ into h₂, and then into dryness x₁. Power plants use this check for turbine steam. Only a few universities teach steam calorimetry; it belongs to advanced steam laboratory work.
prereq: You need dryness fraction, the steam tables, and the steady flow energy equation from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Wet steam at p₁ enters a throttle, a small orifice or valve. It leaves at lower p₂. The process is throttling: no work, negligible heat transfer, small kinetic and potential energy changes. The steady flow energy equation gives h₁ = h₂. h₁ is inlet specific enthalpy, kJ/kg; h₂ is outlet specific enthalpy, kJ/kg.

blocks.where: h_f1 is saturated liquid enthalpy at inlet pressure p₁, kJ/kg; h_fg1 is latent heat at p₁, kJ/kg; x₁ is inlet dryness fraction.

blocks.text: To use this, the outlet must be superheated. Then p₂ and T₂ fix h₂ in the superheated table. At inlet, h₁ = h_f1 + x₁ h_fg1. Substituting h₁ = h₂ gives the formula above.

items: Read inlet pressure p₁, outlet pressure p₂ and outlet temperature T₂.
Confirm the outlet is superheated at p₂ and T₂.
Find h₂ from the superheated steam table.
Find h_f1 and h_fg1 at p₁ from the saturated steam table.

blocks.text: If the outlet is still wet, h₂ depends on an unknown outlet dryness x₂. The equation h₁ = h₂ then has two unknowns, so the throttling calorimeter is invalid.

A separating calorimeter works mechanically. Steam passes through baffles or a centrifuge. Water droplets hit the walls and drain into a measuring vessel. The remaining dry steam is condensed and weighed. Let m_w be separated water mass and m_s be dry steam mass over the same time. Then x = m_s/(m_s + m_w).

This instrument suits very wet steam. It is less exact than a throttling calorimeter and causes pressure loss. A combined separating and throttling calorimeter first removes most water; the throttling part then measures the small remaining wetness.

items: Throttling calorimeter: outlet must be superheated; needs accurate p₁, p₂ and T₂.
Separating calorimeter: direct mass measurement; used when steam is very wet.
Combined unit: separating part handles bulk water, throttling part gives fine dryness.
Both need steady flow and a representative steam sample.

spec.title: Throttling calorimeter
spec.aria: A rightward block diagram of a throttling calorimeter: wet steam at 10 bar passes a throttle of constant enthalpy, enters a chamber at 1 bar, leaves superheated at 130 degrees Celsius, and gives dryness 0.979.

examples.question: Wet steam at 10 bar is throttled to 1 bar and 130°C. At 10 bar, h_f = 762.6 kJ/kg and h_fg = 2015.3 kJ/kg. At 1 bar and 130°C, h = 2736 kJ/kg. Find the inlet dryness fraction x₁.
steps: Check the outlet state: at 1 bar the saturation temperature is about 99.6°C, so 130°C is superheated.
Read the outlet enthalpy: h₂ = 2736 kJ/kg.
At 10 bar: h_f1 = 762.6 kJ/kg and h_fg1 = 2015.3 kJ/kg.

traps: Using h₁ = h₂ when the outlet is still wet. Then h₂ contains unknown x₂ and the calculation cannot give x₁.
Forgetting to check that the outlet is superheated. A temperature alone does not fix h₂ inside the wet region.
Taking h_f and h_fg at the outlet pressure. Both must be at the inlet pressure p₁.
Swapping h_f and h_fg in x₁ = (h₂ − h_f1)/h_fg1. h_fg1 is the latent heat, not the sensible part.
Applying h₁ = h₂ with large kinetic or potential energy changes. The throttle must be well insulated and changes small.

quiz.q: State the enthalpy relation used by a throttling calorimeter.
quiz.a: For steady throttling with no work, little heat loss and small kinetic and potential energy changes, h₁ = h₂.

quiz.q: Why must the outlet of a throttling calorimeter be superheated?
quiz.a: Only then do p₂ and T₂ fix h₂ from the superheated table. If the outlet is wet, h₂ also depends on an unknown x₂.

quiz.q: Wet steam at 10 bar (h_f = 762.6 kJ/kg, h_fg = 2015.3 kJ/kg) is throttled to 1 bar, 120°C, where h = 2716 kJ/kg. Find x₁.
A throttling calorimeter test gives an outlet that is still wet. What should you conclude?
quiz.a: The test is invalid for finding x₁. Use a separating calorimeter or a combined separating and throttling calorimeter.

quiz.q: Write the dryness fraction from a separating calorimeter in terms of masses.
quiz.a: x = m_s/(m_s + m_w), where m_s is dry steam mass and m_w is separated water mass.

quiz.q: Why is a separating calorimeter preferred for very wet steam?
quiz.a: Very wet steam may not become superheated after throttling, so the throttling calorimeter fails. The separating calorimeter removes water and measures masses directly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Power plants use continuous steam-quality instruments based on throttling, separation or light scattering. Combined separating and throttling calorimeters appear in older laboratory manuals and in some boiler test codes. Newer work uses acoustic and optical methods for wet-steam measurement. Search for 'throttling calorimeter', 'separating calorimeter' and 'steam quality measurement'.
